goal: Import Little Navmap .lnmpln flight plans as the expected route of a trip, so tracked flights are pre-logged as legs of that trip with a known destination and predicted route.
frozen_decisions: XML parsing uses fast-xml-parser as a new server runtime dependency. No hand-rolled XML parse.

Leg auto-matching is scoped by an explicit 'active trip' flag; only unflown planned legs of the one active trip are candidates. Manual link/unlink exists as an escape hatch and ships BEFORE auto-matching.
No test framework is introduced. Verification is by running the app, by curl against endpoints, by sqlite3 against the database, and by two ts-node CLI inspectors written as part of the work.

Imported batches are ordered by chaining each leg destination ident to the next leg departure ident, applied only when the chain resolves uniquely across the batch, falling back to upload order with a warning otherwise. Upload order alone is not trustworthy: Little Navmap names files "VFR <depname> (ICAO) to <destname> (ICAO).lnmpln", so a file picker sorted alphabetically can hand the server a batch in reverse route order. A round trip A->B / B->A does not resolve uniquely and must fall back.
sequencing_rationale: The two places this feature can hurt are the parser's tolerance of real files and a wrong auto-match at takeoff. Both are isolated into pure modules with their own ts-node CLI inspectors (src/inspect-lnmpln.ts, src/inspect-legmatch.ts) so they are falsifiable without MSFS and without a test framework.
Manual link/unlink (phase 3) ships before auto-matching (phase 4) on purpose: the escape hatch must exist before anything automatic can attach a flight to the wrong leg.
Map rendering (phase 2) is placed before the linking work because it is low-risk, needs only trip -> planned legs, and pays off the import immediately if the user stops there.

Each phase is gated by a reviewer task, and every task in phase N depends on the reviewer of phase N-1. This is what guarantees that tasks with overlapping allowed_paths across phases can never run concurrently; only within-phase parallelism exists, and every within-phase parallel pair has disjoint allowed_paths.

Type-file ownership is assigned deliberately: parse-shape types live in src/lnmpln.ts and persisted row types in src/types.ts, so the parser task and the DB task in phase 1 can run in parallel without touching the same file.

phases.name: Import and list planned legs
phases.ships: A .lnmpln file (or several at once) can be imported into a trip and its planned legs are listed in the trip's legs table alongside flown flights.

phases.name: Planned route on the trip map
phases.ships: The imported route is drawn on the trip map, visually distinct from flown tracks. A trip that has only planned legs and no flights now shows a map.

phases.name: Active trip and manual link/unlink
phases.ships: One trip can be marked active, and any flight can be manually linked to or unlinked from a planned leg. The escape hatch exists before anything automatic does.

phases.name: Automatic leg matching at takeoff
phases.ships: Taking off near a planned leg's departure while that trip is active automatically attaches the new flight to that leg and trip, and the flight page shows the planned route under the flown track.

phases.name: Live awareness, route progress, export
phases.ships: The live panel names the current planned leg and what remains of it, the trip journey measures progress along the planned route, and planned legs appear in the trip PDF.

tasks.title: Freeze the planned-leg data model, the LNMPLN parse contract and the phase-1 REST surface
definition_of_done: design/data-model.md specifies CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS DDL for planned_legs, planned_waypoints and planned_alternates: every column, its type, nullability, default and index, written in the same style as the statements already in initDb().

It states which columns (if any) are added to existing tables, and confirms each is applied with the PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN idiom already used in src/db.ts. No column is renamed, retyped or dropped.

It states the ON DELETE behaviour for trips -> planned_legs and planned_legs -> planned_waypoints/planned_alternates, given that initDb() sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, and says explicitly what happens to a planned leg when its trip is deleted.

It declares the ParsedFlightPlan TypeScript interface (the parser's output) and states that it lives in src/lnmpln.ts, while persisted row types live in src/types.ts. This split is required so that T-002 and T-003 can run in parallel without editing the same file.

Every one of the 12 format traps listed in intake.md maps to a named field or a stated rule in ParsedFlightPlan: at minimum isSnippet (non-AIRPORT endpoints), cruiseAltFt (CruisingAltF preferred over CruisingAlt), remarks (Comment or Description accepted), createdAt (normalised two-digit-offset timestamp), and approxDistanceNm carrying an explicit 'approximate' flag because procedure waypoints are never present in the file.

It specifies the phase-1 REST surface: method, path, request body/multipart shape, success response shape and error status codes for import (multiple files in one request), list, get one, delete one and reorder. Paths are chosen so literal segments are registrable before the existing /:id routes and before the SPA catch-all.

It states whether planned legs and their waypoints are embedded in the GET /api/trips/:id payload or fetched from a separate endpoint, and gives the reason (payload size vs round trips), because both the trip page and the trip map consume it.
It states the batch-import failure policy: whether one bad file fails the whole request or the response reports per-file outcomes.
It contains no implementation code beyond interface stubs and DDL.

It specifies the batch ordering rule (design.md §9.2): destination-ident-to-departure-ident chaining, the uniqueness condition under which it is applied, the fallback to upload order, and the warning returned to the client when the chain does not resolve. It states how seq is assigned in each case.
risks: Over-modelling: SID/STAR/approach names are worth storing as text on the leg, but modelling procedure legs as first-class rows would be speculative, since the file never contains their waypoints.
Embedding waypoints in the trip payload could bloat GET /api/trips/:id for a long trip; the decision needs to be made here rather than discovered in the client.

Chain resolution is ambiguous for any batch containing a round trip or a repeated field pairing; the contract must define uniqueness precisely enough that T-004 can implement the refusal rather than guess an order.
tasks.model_rationale: Freezes contracts for the whole feature; ambiguous and cross-cutting.

tasks.title: LNMPLN parser module, fast-xml-parser dependency, fixtures and a CLI inspector
frozen_contracts: T-001: ParsedFlightPlan interface and the trap-to-field mapping
definition_of_done: fast-xml-parser is in package.json dependencies (not devDependencies) with a caret-pinned version, and package-lock.json is updated by a real npm install.

src/lnmpln.ts exports a parse function returning exactly the ParsedFlightPlan shape frozen in T-001, and imports nothing from ./db and nothing from fs: it takes a string or Buffer and returns a value. Verify with grep that the module has no database or filesystem import.

samples/lnmpln/ contains the four REAL Little Navmap 3.0.18 exports supplied by the user - the VFR trio KSBA->KMRY, KMRY->KSTS, KSTS->KACV, and the IFR KSFO->KLAX - and all four parse: npx ts-node src/inspect-lnmpln.ts over them reports the correct departure and destination idents, waypoint counts of 7, 5, 6 and 3 respectively, and cruise altitudes of 7500, 2500, 3500 and 27000 ft.

The IFR fixture round-trips its full procedure set through the parser: SID WESLA5 / runway 28L / transition SUSEY; STAR IRNMN2 / runway 24R / transition BURGL; approach KLAX24R / runway 24R / type CUSTOM / CustomDistance 3.00 / CustomAltitude 1000.00 / CustomOffsetAngle 0.00. Every one of those values reaches the ParsedFlightPlan; none is silently dropped.

THE XSD IS NOT AN EXHAUSTIVE DESCRIPTION OF WHAT LITTLE NAVMAP WRITES. <CustomOffsetAngle> appears in the real IFR file and is absent from the XSD copy at .claude/runs/2026-09-04-lnmpln-trip-planner/lnmpln.xsd, whose Approach declares exactly nine children and does not include it. The same gap affects SID, which the XSD gives only Name/Runway/Transition while the manual documents a Type=CUSTOMDEPART variant with CustomDistance. The parser must therefore read by tag name and tolerate elements the XSD does not declare, and must never validate-and-reject on the grounds that an element is undocumented.
No acceptance check anywhere in this task is expressed as conformance to the XSD; correctness is judged against the real files and the manual, with the XSD treated as a partial guide.

The four real files cover only part of the trap list, so these SYNTHESIZED fixtures are still required and must be added alongside them, each named so its purpose is obvious: a UTF-8 BOM-prefixed file (trap 11); two separate <Waypoints> blocks and two <Alternates> blocks (trap 4); ANY file containing an <Alternates> block at all, since no real file has one (trap 4 and the alternates path generally); <Comment> in Header and Waypoint plus a second file using <Description> in both (trap 2 - neither tag appears in any real file); a Waypoint placing its remark after <Pos>, deviating from XSD element order (trap 3); a snippet whose first and last Waypoint Type is not AIRPORT (trap 6 - all eight real endpoints are AIRPORT); a Waypoint whose <Pos> has no Alt attribute (trap 8 - every real Pos carries Alt); a Header whose CruisingAlt and CruisingAltF DISAGREE (trap 9 - all four real files agree, so no real fixture can prove which field the parser read); a two-digit-offset CreationDate of the form 2020-09-11T18:05:15+02 (trap 10 - all four real files use a full -03:00 offset that Date parses natively); an XML comment block including the nested/unbalanced one from the manual (trap 7); a <Departure> element with a parking Start and Type (trap 12 - absent from all four real files); a published non-custom approach carrying ARINC, Suffix and TransitionType; and every rejection path from the malformed-input line below.

The parser tolerates <AircraftPerformance> with no <FilePath> child: all three real files carry only <Type> and <Name>, though intake.md lists FilePath among its children. A missing FilePath is not an error.

The parser preserves ident strings as strings across all three real files: KSBA, KMRY, KSTS, KACV and en-route idents such as SUDDO, OINGO, ZORAN, HMPBK, GIPVY are never coerced to numbers or booleans.

npx ts-node src/inspect-lnmpln.ts samples/lnmpln/*.lnmpln prints, per file: departure ident and type, destination ident and type, cruise altitude in feet, waypoint count, alternate count, isSnippet, and exits 0. [CORRECTED 2026-09-05: name the three trip files explicitly, do NOT glob. A fifth real file (VFR Monterey Rgnl (KMRY) to San Francisco Intl (KSFO).lnmpln) also matches VFR* and gives KMRY two successors, so that glob now correctly returns AMBIGUOUS_SUCCESSOR. The fixture directory is expected to grow; a glob silently changes what the assertion means.]
The two-block fixture reports the sum of both blocks' waypoints, in document order, proving the maxOccurs=unbounded concatenation.
A fixture where CruisingAlt and CruisingAltF disagree reports the CruisingAltF value.
A CreationDate of the form 2020-09-11T18:05:15+02 is printed as a valid ISO instant, not Invalid Date.
The official example's nested/unbalanced XML comment block around the custom SID does not break the parse.

Malformed input is rejected with a one-line reason and a non-zero exit, never a stack trace or a partial object, for each of: input that is not XML; XML with no <Flightplan>; a plan with zero waypoints; a waypoint with Lat=91; a waypoint with Lon=-181. Add these as samples/lnmpln/synthetic/bad-*.lnmpln.
Waypoints are read by tag name, never by position, so the fixture that puts Description after Pos parses identically to one that does not.
npx tsc --noEmit passes.
The NavData cycle is read per file and not assumed constant across a logbook: the VFR trio carries Cycle="1801" and the IFR file Cycle="2609".

CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (Orchestrator): the chain-sort demonstration globs samples/lnmpln/VFR*.lnmpln, not all four real files. The all-four glob is EXPECTED to report NO_UNIQUE_HEAD because the IFR plan belongs to a different trip and gives the batch two heads. Do not treat that as a failure and do not make the all-four glob chain. [CORRECTED 2026-09-05: name the three trip files explicitly, do NOT glob. A fifth real file (VFR Monterey Rgnl (KMRY) to San Francisco Intl (KSFO).lnmpln) also matches VFR* and gives KMRY two successors, so that glob now correctly returns AMBIGUOUS_SUCCESSOR. The fixture directory is expected to grow; a glob silently changes what the assertion means.]

CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (Orchestrator): synthesized fixtures, including every bad-*.lnmpln, live in samples/lnmpln/synthetic/. The top level of samples/lnmpln/ holds ONLY genuine Little Navmap exports, because samples/lnmpln/*.lnmpln is written into acceptance criteria and their original filenames are load-bearing evidence for the ordering defect. [CORRECTED 2026-09-05: name the three trip files explicitly, do NOT glob. A fifth real file (VFR Monterey Rgnl (KMRY) to San Francisco Intl (KSFO).lnmpln) also matches VFR* and gives KMRY two successors, so that glob now correctly returns AMBIGUOUS_SUCCESSOR. The fixture directory is expected to grow; a glob silently changes what the assertion means.]
risks: PARTLY RETIRED, FURTHER REDUCED BY THE IFR FILE: four genuine Little Navmap 3.0.18 exports now sit in samples/lnmpln/. Real data now covers the parse happy path, procedures (SID, STAR and a CUSTOM approach), both IFR and VFR flightplan types, a short 3-waypoint route, and two different NavData cycles. What remains synthetic is still substantial: multiple <Waypoints> blocks, alternates of any kind (no real file has an <Alternates> block), the two-digit CreationDate offset, a BOM, XML comments, a missing Pos/@Alt, a <Departure> element, a published non-custom approach, and every rejection path. All four files are still one program version and one region.

LOWERED: the Designer frozen fast-xml-parser config was prototyped against all three real files and parses them correctly - idents stay strings, the isArray jpaths resolve, and the full-offset CreationDate parses natively. The residual concern is narrower than originally scored but not gone: a single-element <Waypoints> block collapsing to an object rather than an array is still only exercised by a synthesized fixture, and the config has never been run against an IFR plan with procedures.
tasks.model_rationale: Highest-risk task in the plan. New module + dependency + geo extraction + 13 format traps + UNKNOWN_ELEMENT + chain-sort. A silent mis-parse is residual risk #1.

tasks.title: Planned-leg schema migration and CRUD in src/db.ts
frozen_contracts: T-001: DDL, ON DELETE behaviour, persisted row types
design.md Amendment B: widened procedure columns on planned_legs
definition_of_done: initDb() creates the three new tables with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS per the T-001 DDL, and their indexes with CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS.
Starting the server twice against the same flights.db produces no error; sqlite3 flights.db ".schema planned_legs" shows one definition.

Starting the server against a copy of the existing flights.db upgrades it in place: sqlite3 copy.db "select count(*) from planned_legs" returns 0, and select count(*) from flights and from trips return the same numbers as before the upgrade.
src/types.ts gains the persisted row types from T-001; no existing exported type loses or changes a field.
Exported functions cover: create a leg with its waypoints and alternates, list legs for a trip in seq order with children attached, get one leg, delete one leg, reorder legs within a trip.

Creating a leg is wrapped in a single better-sqlite3 transaction: force a failure partway (e.g. a deliberately invalid waypoint) and confirm with sqlite3 that no planned_waypoints rows survive for that leg.
deleteTrip() on a trip that has planned legs still returns true, and sqlite3 flights.db "select count(*) from planned_legs where trip_id not in (select id from trips)" returns 0.
GET /api/trips and GET /api/flights return the same shapes as before (additive fields only), confirmed by curl before and after.
No function in this task reads or writes flights.flight_plan_name or the flight_plans/ directory.

The procedure columns on planned_legs cover the full approach record, not just its name: approach type, arinc, suffix, transition_type, custom_distance, custom_altitude and custom_offset_angle, plus the SID type and custom_distance, per design.md Amendment B. The earlier nine-column freeze had no home for a CUSTOM approach type or any of its three Custom* values, so a stored row could not distinguish a custom runway-extension approach from a published one.
Every added procedure column is nullable and applied additively, since the three VFR fixtures have no <Procedures> block at all and must continue to import with all of them NULL.
Verifiable with sqlite3: after importing a plan with no procedures, select on the procedure columns returns NULL for every one of them, and the leg is otherwise complete.
risks: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON is already set, so a REFERENCES clause on the new tables is genuinely enforced. A leg row inserted with a trip_id that does not exist will now throw where the older unconstrained flights.trip_id would not have. The import endpoint must therefore validate the trip exists first (T-004).
A cascade from trips is the right default but makes trip deletion destroy imported plans silently; the UI must warn (T-005/T-013).

The procedure column set is driven by one real IFR file plus the manual. A published (non-custom) approach with ARINC, Suffix and TransitionType populated is still unseen in real data, so those three columns are modelled on documentation alone.
tasks.model_rationale: Wide but fully specified: schema.sql gives 3 tables, 18 procedure columns, 4 ALTER steps and the cascade verbatim. Mechanical against a frozen DDL.

tasks.title: REST endpoints: LNMPLN import (multi-file) and planned-leg CRUD
frozen_contracts: T-001: REST surface, batch-import failure policy, response shapes
T-001/design.md §9.2: batch ordering rule, uniqueness condition, fallback and warning
definition_of_done: The import endpoint accepts one or many .lnmpln files in a single multipart request and returns 201 with the created legs in the shape frozen in T-001.

A separate multer instance (or separate limits) is used for LNMPLN uploads; the existing 20 MB MAX_FLIGHT_PLAN_BYTES PDF limit is untouched, and the LNMPLN limit is far smaller and stated in the code.

Rejections return { error: string } with a proper status, matching the existing handlers' style, for: no file; a file that is not XML; a file the parser refuses; a file over the size limit; a trip id that does not exist (404); a malformed id (400).

The batch failure policy frozen in T-001 is implemented and observable: a request mixing one good and one bad file produces exactly the documented outcome, and the response names the failing file and the reason.
Imported batches are ordered by chaining destination ident to departure ident, not by multipart upload order, per design.md §9.2. seq is assigned from the resolved chain.

RESOLVING CASE, verifiable against the real fixtures and the sharpest regression test this feature has: POST the three real files from samples/lnmpln/ in ALPHABETICAL filename order (which is KSTS->KACV, KMRY->KSTS, KSBA->KMRY, exactly the reverse of the route) into an empty trip, then run a single query - sqlite3 flights.db "select seq, <departure ident col>, <destination ident col> from planned_legs where trip_id = <id> order by seq" using the column names from the T-001 DDL. It must return exactly three rows: 1 KSBA KMRY, 2 KMRY KSTS, 3 KSTS KACV.

FALLBACK CASE: a batch whose chain does not resolve uniquely - at minimum a round trip (import KSBA->KMRY together with a hand-made KMRY->KSBA) and a batch of two unrelated legs that share no idents - is stored in upload order, and the response carries a warning naming the reason. Verify with the same sqlite3 query that seq follows upload order in both.
The warning is a warning, not an error: the fallback import still returns success and still creates the legs, so a batch that cannot be chained is never silently dropped.
Re-importing the same three files into a second trip produces the same resolved order, proving the sort does not depend on filesystem or multipart field ordering.
All new literal routes are registered before the existing /:id routes and before app.get('*'); curl -sS on every new path returns JSON with a JSON content-type, never the SPA index.html.
GET returns legs in seq order with waypoints and alternates attached.
DELETE removes a leg and its children; a repeated DELETE returns 404; sqlite3 confirms no orphan waypoint rows remain.
The reorder endpoint changes seq, and a subsequent GET returns the new order.
Regression check on the unrelated PDF feature: POST, GET and DELETE of a PDF against /api/flights/:id/flight-plan still work and flights.flight_plan_name is set and cleared as before.
The task records a copy-pasteable curl transcript covering import, list, delete, reorder and three rejection cases.

PROCEDURE ROUND-TRIP, verifiable against the real IFR fixture with one query: import "IFR San Francisco Intl (KSFO) to Los Angeles Intl (KLAX).lnmpln", then sqlite3 flights.db "select <sid cols>, <star cols>, <approach cols> from planned_legs where trip_id = <id>" using the column names from the T-003 DDL. It must return WESLA5, 28L, SUSEY for the SID; IRNMN2, 24R, BURGL for the STAR; and KLAX24R, 24R, CUSTOM, 3.0, 1000.0, 0.0 for the approach name, runway, type, custom distance, custom altitude and custom offset angle. A NULL in any of those twelve values is a failure.

The IFR fixture does not chain with the VFR trio, and a batch mixing them falls back with reason NO_UNIQUE_HEAD rather than inventing an order. Verify by importing all four files in one request and confirming the fallback warning names that reason and that all four legs are still created in upload order.
The IFR file imports as its own trip, separate from the VFR trip, and legs belonging to the two trips never interleave.

NOTE 2026-09-04 (Orchestrator, after review finding F-8): DoD 15 asks for a curl transcript, but this task allowed_paths is ["src/server.ts"], so it had nowhere to write one. The intent — every endpoint exercised against a real server — was satisfied: T-004 reported the transcript in its response envelope and the phase-1 Reviewer independently reproduced import, list, delete, reorder and the rejection cases. Future tasks that must PRODUCE an artifact need a reports path in allowed_paths.
risks: Route ordering is a known trap in this file; a new route registered after app.get('*') will silently return HTML and look like a client bug.
Multer errors surface through the existing error middleware; a new upload limit must produce a JSON error, not an HTML stack page.

Chain-sorting is inference, not fact. It is right for the common case and wrong for a genuine out-and-back flown in one direction only; the fallback plus the reorder endpoint from this same task are what make a wrong inference cheap to correct.
tasks.model_rationale: Endpoint shapes, statuses and the batch-import policy are frozen in §7.1. Integrates chain-sort rather than deciding it.

tasks.title: Draw the planned route on the trip map, distinct from flown tracks
frozen_contracts: T-001: planned-leg JSON payload shape including waypoints
definition_of_done: TripMap takes an optional planned-legs prop; when it is omitted the component renders exactly as it does today, so every existing caller (including PrintTrip) is unaffected.
Planned routes render as dashed polylines in a colour clearly outside the LEG_COLORS palette, drawn beneath the flown tracks, with a tooltip naming the planned leg and its route.
Waypoints render as small markers showing their ident on hover.

The bounds controller fits over flown points and planned waypoints together, so a trip with planned legs but no flights shows a fitted map instead of the current 'No GPS points recorded for this trip.' message.
A trip with flights and no planned legs is pixel-comparable to before the change.
The trip PDF export still works: /print/trip/:id renders and GET /api/trips/:id/export.pdf returns a PDF containing the flown tracks, unchanged.
A planned leg crossing the antimeridian does not draw a polyline wrapping the wrong way round the world, or the limitation is documented in a comment if leaflet's default handling is accepted.
npm run build:client completes with no TypeScript errors.

EXPECTED-BEHAVIOUR RULE, not a defect: where a plan has procedures, the drawn planned route will visibly diverge from the flown track at both ends. LNM never writes procedure waypoints, so the en-route skeleton is close to a straight line between the airports - in the real IFR fixture, KSFO to EBAYE to KLAX measures 293.5 nm against a direct great circle of 293.2 nm, a 0.08 percent excess - while the real aircraft curves away through the SID at one end and the STAR and approach at the other. This divergence must be left visible and must NOT be corrected by snapping, interpolating or otherwise fitting the planned line to the flown track. Where the leg has a SID, STAR or approach, the UI says so, so the gap reads as missing procedure data rather than a drawing error.
risks: MapReadySignal drives the PDF export's readiness detection. Adding layers that load asynchronously could delay or break the 'ready' signal and hang the Puppeteer render; verify the export still settles.
Antimeridian wrapping is a real hazard for exactly the kind of long-haul trip this feature targets.

A reviewer or a later dispatcher seeing the planned line depart from the flown track at both ends will reasonably read it as a rendering bug. The DoD line above exists to stop that: any change making the two lines agree at the ends is a regression, not a fix.
tasks.model_rationale: Leaflet rendering against frozen §6.2 divergence rules.

tasks.title: Freeze the active-trip semantics, the flight-to-leg link, and the auto-match algorithm
definition_of_done: design/matching.md states where the active-trip flag lives (a column on trips or a single-row settings table), and gives the exact statement sequence that guarantees at most one active trip at any time.
It defines the flight-to-planned-leg link: which table holds it, and its uniqueness rules (a planned leg has at most one flight; a flight has at most one planned leg).
It specifies that unlink restores prior state: whether trip_id was set by the auto-link is recorded, so unlinking restores the flight's previous trip_id instead of blindly nulling it.

It gives the auto-match algorithm as a pure function signature: inputs (takeoff lat/lon, timestamp, aircraft type, the candidate legs) and output (a chosen leg id, or null together with a reason code from a named enum).

It states the departure-radius threshold in nautical miles and justifies it against the fact that FlightManager.startFlight() only fires once the aircraft is already airborne (airspeed > 30 kts for 3 debounce frames), so the reported position can be several miles from the field.

It enumerates every refusal rule explicitly: no active trip; the leg is already flown; the leg is already linked to another flight; the flight is already manually linked; two or more candidate legs are within the radius (ambiguous, refuse rather than guess); the leg is a snippet with no departure airport.
It defines the landing behaviour: what happens when the arrival is far from the planned destination (keep the link and flag a deviation, or unlink), and what the user is shown.
It states that matching must run once per flight start, must not add per-frame cost, and must not perform a second linear scan of the ~40k-row airport table per frame.
It states the restart behaviour: the link is persisted at takeoff, so a server restart mid-flight loses nothing.
It lists the reason codes verbatim, so both the API and the UI can explain a refusal instead of failing silently.
It contains no implementation code beyond the function signature and the reason-code enum.
risks: The dangerous default is a generous radius that silently attaches a flight to the wrong leg. The contract should bias hard toward refusing: an unlinked flight is a small annoyance, a wrongly linked one corrupts a trip's record and the user may not notice.

Two legs departing the same airport (a there-and-back trip, or a multi-day trip returning to base) is not an edge case in this domain, it is the common case. The ambiguity rule carries most of the weight here.
tasks.model_rationale: Freezes matcher semantics; the high-consequence half of the design.

tasks.title: Pure leg-matching module with a scenario CLI harness
frozen_contracts: T-010: function signature, radius threshold, refusal rules, reason codes
definition_of_done: src/legMatcher.ts exports the pure function with the signature frozen in T-010 and performs no database, filesystem or network access; verified by grep showing no import of ./db, ./airports, fs or http.
Every refusal path returns the documented reason code from T-010; no path returns a bare null with no reason.
npx ts-node src/inspect-legmatch.ts runs a scenario table printing expected versus actual for each case and exits non-zero if any case disagrees.

The scenario table includes at minimum: an exact match over the field; a takeoff 8 nm out on climb (matches); a takeoff 40 nm away (refuses, out of radius); two candidate legs departing the same airport (refuses, ambiguous); a leg already flown (refuses); a leg already linked (refuses); no active trip (refuses); a snippet leg with no departure airport (refuses); and an antimeridian pair such as NZAA to NFFN where a naive longitude difference computes a wrong distance.

The scenario table draws its coordinates from the four real fixtures wherever it can, so thresholds are exercised against genuine airport positions: KSBA, KMRY, KSTS and KACV from the VFR trip and KSFO and KLAX from the IFR plan. KMRY appearing as both a destination and a departure gives a real test that an already-flown leg is excluded while its successor remains a candidate.

The AMBIGUOUS case stays SYNTHETIC and must be constructed by hand: no two of the real legs depart the same field, so the real fixtures cannot exercise the refusal that matters most. The scenario table must state this in a comment so a later reader does not mistake real coverage for complete coverage.
The antimeridian case is asserted explicitly, because raw-degree distance maths is the classic silent failure here.
The module does not modify src/flightManager.ts; integration is T-016.
npx tsc --noEmit passes.

The IFR fixture adds a real long-leg case (293 nm KSFO to KLAX) alongside the short VFR hops, so the radius constants are exercised at both ends of the range rather than one. It adds no ambiguity coverage: KSFO and KLAX collide with none of the VFR fields either.
risks: HIGHEST-CONSEQUENCE MODULE IN THE FEATURE. A false positive attaches a flight to the wrong leg and corrupts a trip's record; a false negative merely means the user links it by hand. The scenario table should be written to make false positives fail loudly.
The thresholds chosen here are guesses until real MSFS takeoffs are observed; make them named constants with a comment stating what they were calibrated against.

The real fixtures make the matching happy path concrete but give zero coverage of the ambiguity refusal, which is the path that prevents silent data corruption. Coverage of that path is exactly as synthetic as it was before the files arrived.
tasks.model_rationale: A wrong match silently corrupts a trip record. Refusal precedence and ambiguity handling are subtle and adversarial.

EXPECTED-BEHAVIOUR RULE, not a defect: where a plan has procedures, the drawn planned route will visibly diverge from the flown track at both ends. LNM never writes procedure waypoints, so the en-route skeleton is close to a straight line between the airports - in the real IFR fixture, KSFO to EBAYE to KLAX measures 293.5 nm against a direct great circle of 293.2 nm, a 0.08 percent excess - while the real aircraft curves away through the SID at one end and the STAR and approach at the other. This divergence must be left visible and must NOT be corrected by snapping, interpolating or otherwise fitting the planned line to the flown track. Where the leg has a SID, STAR or approach, the UI says so, so the gap reads as missing procedure data rather than a drawing error.
risks: This is the screen where a user will notice a wrong auto-match; the unlink control being one click away is what makes phase 4 safe to ship.
This is the screen where the end-divergence is most visible, since a single flight fills the map, so the temptation to snap the planned line to the track is strongest here.

tasks.model_rationale: Three well-specified fixes against findings with reproductions.

global_risks: PARTLY RETIRED (2026-09-04, twice): four genuine Little Navmap 3.0.18 exports now sit in samples/lnmpln/ - a VFR trio chaining into one trip (KSBA to KMRY to KSTS to KACV) and a separate IFR plan (KSFO to KLAX, FL270). Real data now covers the parse happy path, both flightplan types, a full <Procedures> block with a CUSTOM approach, routes from 3 to 7 waypoints, and two NavData cycles. What survives is narrower but real: no file has an <Alternates> block, a <Departure> element, multiple <Waypoints> blocks, a BOM, an XML comment, a missing Pos/@Alt, a two-digit CreationDate offset, or disagreeing CruisingAlt/CruisingAltF, and none of the eight endpoints is a non-airport. Those, every rejection path, and a published non-custom approach remain covered only by fixtures we wrote ourselves. All four files are also one program version and one region.

Auto-matching at takeoff is the only place this feature can silently corrupt existing data. It is deliberately sequenced last among the behavioural phases, behind a working manual unlink, behind a pure module with a scenario harness, and behind an adversarial review.

There is no test framework and none is being added, so the two ts-node inspectors are the entire regression net for the parser and the matcher. They should be kept runnable and referenced in the README, or they will rot.
flights.db is live user data with a WAL. Every schema rehearsal must run against a checkpointed copy, never the working database.
Two features are called 'flight plan' in this codebase. Every task above that touches user-facing strings or the export path carries an explicit non-conflation check.

Batch ordering is inferred rather than declared. The chain-sort exists because Little Navmap filenames sort alphabetically into an order unrelated to the route, and the three real fixtures demonstrate this precisely: alphabetically they arrive in exact reverse. The inference is right for a linear trip and wrong for an out-and-back, which is why the fallback, the warning and the manual reorder all have to work.

The XSD at .claude/runs/2026-09-04-lnmpln-trip-planner/lnmpln.xsd is NOT an exhaustive description of what Little Navmap writes. The real IFR file contains <CustomOffsetAngle>, which the XSD Approach does not declare among its nine children; the XSD SID likewise declares only Name/Runway/Transition while the manual documents a Type=CUSTOMDEPART variant with CustomDistance. Any task that treats the XSD as complete will drop real data silently. Read by tag name, tolerate undeclared elements, and never reject an element for being undocumented.
open_questions: ANSWERED (2026-09-04): four real .lnmpln files are now in samples/lnmpln/, including the IFR export with procedures that was the outstanding ask. The remaining fixture gaps are narrower and mostly cannot be produced by flying: a plan with <Alternates>, a plan saved from a parking position so it carries <Departure>, and a file from an older Little Navmap version. Ask the user for those only if cheap; otherwise synthesize and accept the residual risk.
What departure radius feels right in practice? T-010 must pick a number, but it can only be calibrated once real takeoffs are observed; expect one tuning pass after phase 4 ships.
Should importing a plan whose departure matches an already-flown flight in the same trip offer to link them retroactively? Out of scope as planned, but a natural follow-up once phase 3 exists.

Should the chain-sort also run when legs are added to a trip that already has planned legs, chaining onto the existing tail rather than only within the uploaded batch? Out of scope as planned - T-004 chains within the batch only - but it is the obvious next question the first time someone imports leg 4 of a trip on its own.

How should a leg with procedures present its distance? The en-route skeleton understates the flown route by the length of the SID, STAR and approach, which the file never contains. T-005 already labels such distances approximate; whether to additionally show that procedures are present, so the reader knows WHY it is approximate, is a UX call worth making once real legs are on screen.

Folded the §9.2 batch-ordering defect into the plan and reshaped the fixture risk now that three real .lnmpln files have arrived. Added the chain-sort as a frozen decision. T-001 gains a DoD line requiring the ordering rule, uniqueness condition, fallback and warning to be specified. T-004 owns the implementation and carries the sharpest regression test in the feature: importing the three real files in alphabetical order (which is exact reverse route order) must yield seq 1,2,3 = KSBA->KMRY, KMRY->KSTS, KSTS->KACV from one sqlite3 query, plus a fallback case covering a round trip. T-005 surfaces the fallback warning and the manual reorder. T-006 and T-018 now use the real three-leg trip as their integration scenario instead of synthesized data. Beyond the traps the Orchestrator listed (4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12), inspection of the files shows traps 2, 3, 6 and 9 are ALSO still synthetic: no <Comment> or <Description> appears in any of the three, no waypoint deviates from XSD element order, all six endpoints are AIRPORT, and CruisingAlt equals CruisingAltF in all three so no real fixture can prove the parser reads the float. Also noted: <AircraftPerformance> in all three carries no <FilePath> child, though intake.md lists it. No task ids were renumbered and no task was added or removed.

Independently verified while amending: CustomOffsetAngle is absent from the XSD Approach (which declares exactly nine children), the XSD SID also omits the documented Type/CustomDistance so the gap is not unique to Approach, no real file has an <Alternates> or <Departure> element, cycles are 1801 (x3) and 2609, and the skeleton-versus-great-circle figures recompute to 293.48 nm against 293.23 nm, a 0.084 percent excess. No task ids renumbered; no task added or removed.
Assigned a model tier and rationale to every task per the new agents.md model-choice rule. Recorded the policy in model_policy. No task, dependency or allowed_path changed.

T-002 DoD corrections after the dispatcher run: bad-* fixtures are under samples/lnmpln/synthetic/, and the chain-sort demonstration globs VFR*.lnmpln since the all-four glob correctly reports NO_UNIQUE_HEAD once the IFR fixture is present. Also approved the additive ParsedFlightPlan provenance fields (simData, navDataSource, navDataCycle) and required UNKNOWN_ELEMENT to scan <Procedures>.

Phase-1 review closed: verdict approve. Ratified T-003 owning the full migration block per reviewer adjudication 2 and narrowed T-011 to the functions only. Recorded that T-004 DoD 15 asked for an artifact the task had no writable path for. Findings F-1 to F-4 dispatched as T-004b; F-5, F-6, F-7 deferred as follow-ups.

Fifth real fixture added by the user (KMRY->KSFO). It breaks the VFR*.lnmpln chain-sort acceptance glob by giving KMRY two successors — correct behaviour, wrong test shape — so the assertion now names the three trip files explicitly. The file also retires three synthetic-only gaps: a published non-custom approach (ILS DUYET, ARINC I28L), a SID Type=CUSTOMDEPART, and a <Departure> element with a Parking start.

Phase-3 review (T-014) returned request_changes with six findings; two required adjudication because the frozen design was self-inconsistent rather than merely unimplemented. Both are written up as design.md Amendment C. (a) The auto-match candidate loader was filtering status NOT IN ('flown','diverted') in SQL, which made design.md §13.2's LEG_ALREADY_FLOWN refusal unreachable in production — measured, a second KSBA takeoff after leg 1 is flown reported NO_LEG_IN_RADIUS at ~160 nm instead of naming the leg 0 nm away. Eligibility now lives only in matcher step 5 and the loader is renamed getPlannedLegCandidatesForActiveTrip. Done before T-015/T-016 exist so no call site needs revisiting and so T-015's harness cannot green-light an unreachable branch. contracts/planned-legs.d.ts and design.md §12.1/§13.5 updated. (b) design.md §16's 'deleteTrip needs no change' held for ordinary trip membership but stranded a flight that a LINK had moved into the trip, discarding planned_leg_prev_trip_id unread — the one path breaking the link's promise to restore. §16 amended. Also ruled: the re-link guard (F-2) belongs in linkFlightToPlannedLeg, not the endpoint, because T-016 calls the db layer directly; and the active-trip control is gated behind planned_legs.length > 0 || is_active === 1, since design.md §13.2 step 2 refuses with NO_PLANNED_LEGS before distance is computed, making the control inert until a plan is imported — which restores T-013 DoD 8 and §18's 'renders exactly as it did before' criterion. No task ids renumbered, none added or removed.

T-014 was run on opus rather than the sonnet the plan assigned. Rationale under the agents.md model-complexity rule: the task grew beyond its planned shape — three tasks across db, HTTP and client, plus two frozen-contract adjudications referred to it by the Orchestrator, against a phase the plan itself calls 'the gate that must not be waved through'. That is the ambiguous/cross-file/high-risk case the rule reserves stronger reasoning for. It paid: the two design self-inconsistencies and the DoD breach were all found by execution — a headless-Chromium render diff against a git worktree at 8cec371, and a measured 160 nm refusal — not by reading the Dispatchers' reports.

Phase-4 review (T-018) returned approve with five findings; no false positive was producible in nine deliberate attempts across two hand-built trips. Actions: (a) added T-024 for finding F-3 — phase 4 writes arrival_deviation_nm on every landing of a linked flight and NOTHING in the client rendered it, while design.md §14 specifies the leg row's contract in full; no remaining planned task touched those files, so §14 would have lapsed silently. This is the review catching a scheduling gap, not a code defect. (b) added T-025 for F-1 (PATCH status:'planned' on a linked flown/diverted leg returns 200 and destroys the deviation while keeping the link — API-only, but phase 4 is what makes the column non-null in the first place), F-2 (nothing would catch a re-introduced status filter in getPlannedLegCandidatesForActiveTrip: inspect-legmatch.ts is pure and never executes the SQL, so an Amendment C revert has no failing symptom), and F-4 (the comment on the deliberately-dead FLIGHT_ALREADY_LINKED path describes a 'manual path' that does not call the matcher; guard stays, comment corrected). (c) F-5 process finding accepted: allowed_paths for T-013, T-016 and T-017 were widened mid-task by the Orchestrator and plan.json still read as though they had not been, so src/db.ts could not be diffed against its phase-3-approved state. The three task entries are now corrected to record what was actually granted. Rule going forward: a widening is an amendment, recorded when granted, not at the end.

model_policy.rule: agents.md: model choice must match task complexity — lighter/faster for simple scoped tasks, stronger reasoning for ambiguous, cross-file or high-risk tasks.

tiers.opus: Ambiguous, cross-file, or high-risk: the parser, the matcher, the FlightManager hook, and the two reviews that gate them.
tiers.sonnet: Scoped work against a frozen contract — schema, endpoints, client, rendering, and the narrower reviews.
tiers.haiku: Not assigned. No task in this plan is both trivial and low-consequence; see notes.

model_policy.notes: Every remaining task either edits shared state or is gated by a contract whose misreading is expensive. The one genuine haiku candidate — writing the synthetic bad-*.lnmpln fixtures — is a sub-part of T-002 and is not worth splitting out purely to fit a tier.
